title: Bad allergy reaction — swelling and trouble breathing
applies_to: Someone who ate, touched, or was stung by something they react badly to, and whose face, lips, or throat is swelling, or who is finding it hard to breathe.

citations.source: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: First Aid
WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020

steps.text: Look at their face, lips, and tongue. Ask if their throat feels tight.
Call for an ambulance now. Say the word allergy, and say the swelling is getting worse.
Ask if they carry an emergency allergy pen that a doctor gave them. Ask them to point to where it is.
Help them use their own pen. Press it firmly into the outer thigh and hold it there for as long as the label on it says.
Help them lie flat with their legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up instead.
Loosen tight clothing at the neck and the waist.
Stay with them. Keep watching their breathing until help arrives.
If they are no better after 5 minutes and a second pen is there, use it the same way and tell the crew.

do_not: Do not let them stand up or walk about. Standing can make this much worse very fast.
Do not wait to see whether it settles on its own.
Do not give them anything to eat or drink.
Do not put anything in their mouth while the throat is swelling.
Do not throw the used pen away. Give it to the ambulance crew.
escalate_if: They stop answering you and stop breathing normally — start pushing on the chest.
Their breathing gets worse, or the lips go blue or grey — say this on the phone right away.
They were stung inside the mouth or the throat — tell the crew, because the airway can close fast.
They feel faint or their skin goes cold and clammy — keep them lying flat with the legs up.
